title: Creatures of the Ruins: Goat-Demons, Lilith and Jackals
lead: When the prophets picture a city under God's judgment, wild things fill its palaces. Jackals, ostriches, owls and hyenas move in. So do stranger beings: the hairy se'irim ("goat-demons") and Lilith (Isaiah 13:19–22; Isaiah 34:11–15). The Hebrew names are hard to pin down. The old translations turned some of the animals into monsters, such as the KJV's "dragons" and "satyrs." They turned one night spirit into a bird: the KJV has "screech owl" for Lilith.

sections.b: Two oracles in Isaiah give the fullest picture. Babylon, "the beauty of the kingdoms," will end like Sodom. Its houses will be "crammed with owls" (Isaiah 13:19–22). Edom's land will be taken over by desert owl and hedgehog, ibis and raven. "It will be a den for jackals, / a haunt of ostriches" (Isaiah 34:13), and "a goat-demon will call out to its fellow" (Isaiah 34:14). The animals mean that people are gone: what humans abandon, the wild takes back. Revelation reuses the scene for the fall of Babylon the Great: "She has become a home for demons" (Revelation 18:2). Jesus speaks of an unclean spirit that "roams through dry country, searching for a place to rest" (Matthew 12:43).

Sa'ir, "hairy one," is the ordinary word for a male goat. But in a few places it names something people worshiped or feared. Israel must stop sacrificing to the se'irim (Leviticus 17:7). Jeroboam appointed priests "for the goat idols and for the calves he had made" (2 Chronicles 11:15). The KJV has "devils" in both verses, and the Greek of Leviticus has "empty things." In Isaiah 13:21 and 34:14 the se'irim dance and call among the ruins. This site's Plain English Translation has "goat-demons." The KJV has "satyrs," the goat-men of Greek myth. The Greek has daimonia, "demons," and the Latin pilosi, "hairy ones." The BSB has "wild goats" instead. So readers divide: real goats among the stones, or goat-shaped spirits of the waste places. The STEPBible lexicon gives "he-goat" for the ordinary word and "satyr" for these verses.

Lilith (lilit) is named once in the Bible: "Lilith, too, will settle there / and find herself a place to rest" (Isaiah 34:14). The STEPBible lexicon defines her as a female night demon "who haunts the desolate places of Edom." It adds that the word might name a night animal. The old translations show the puzzle. The Greek has onokentauroi, "donkey-centaurs." The Latin has lamia. In Latin writers a lamia was a witch said to suck children's blood, but Lewis and Short's Latin dictionary takes the word in this verse as a kind of owl. The KJV has "screech owl." Later Jewish lore made much of her. In the Talmud Rabbi Hanina warns that anyone who sleeps alone in a house will be seized by Lilith (Bavli Shabbat 151b). The Bible gives her no story and no power. She is one more creature of the ruins, resting where God's judgment has emptied the land. See the note and variant on Isaiah 34:14.

sections.h: Jackals, not dragons; ostriches or owls?
sections.b:
Two Hebrew words look alike. Tannim, plural of tan, are jackals, the howling animals of ruined towns (Isaiah 34:13; Jeremiah 9:11; Micah 1:8). Tannin is a different word, for a great sea creature, serpent or dragon (Genesis 1:21; Isaiah 27:1). The KJV printed "dragons" for the jackals again and again (Isaiah 13:22; Isaiah 34:13; Isaiah 35:7; Isaiah 43:20; Jeremiah 9:11; Jeremiah 10:22; Jeremiah 14:6; Jeremiah 49:33; Jeremiah 51:37; Job 30:29; Psalm 44:19; Micah 1:8; Malachi 1:3). The Latin did the same in Isaiah 34:13. But in Lamentations 4:3 the KJV has "sea monsters." There the written Hebrew text has tannin, while the reading marked in the margin has tannim, "jackals," which this site's Plain English Translation follows. The spellings cross the other way too. In Ezekiel 29:3 Pharaoh is the great sea monster, but the Hebrew spells the word tannim. So in a few verses translations divide.

The bird called bat ya'anah, "daughter of the ya'anah," is harder. Most modern translations, such as the BSB, read "ostrich," and so does this site's Plain English Translation (Leviticus 11:16; Job 30:29; Isaiah 13:21). The KJV has "owl." The STEPBible lexicon gives both "owl" and "ostrich," and adds that it may be an extinct bird whose exact meaning is unknown. The Greek of Isaiah 13:21 made the birds "sirens." So the ostrich is the leading guess, not a certainty. Either way, Job's cry is about desert creatures, not monsters: "Jackals are my brothers now, / ostriches my companions" (Job 30:29).
